transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hi. Thank you. I, um, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten completely out of hand at work, and honestly, in my head, too. I'm a production manager at a manufacturing plant—I have my master's in industrial engineering, so I'm used to handling complex systems and a heavy workload, you know? But recently... I don't know, I just had this incredible surge where I was doing absolutely *everything*. 

I mean, I was launching these massive, nonstop plant redesign projects. We're talking complete workflow overhauls on the assembly floor that usually take months of committee meetings, and I was just doing them all at once, drafting the CAD files at my kitchen table at 2 AM. I felt like I had to get it done right then. And I was calling our suppliers way after hours—like, I'd be on the phone with our raw materials vendors at 11 PM, or midnight, because I just couldn't wait until morning. My mind was just moving so fast with all these structural improvements we needed to make right that second. I even completely rewrote the entire quarterly shift plan for the floor staff by myself. I just felt like I was the only one who could see how it all needed to fit together, and I was so driven, just pushing and pushing everybody and myself. 

But then... it's like I hit a wall. A massive, concrete wall. And I came in today because I went from doing all of that, running on all cylinders, to suddenly being completely unable to keep up with the very plans I had just set in motion. I look at the project timelines I made just a little while ago and I can't even process them. I can barely drag myself in to oversee the redesigns I forced everyone to start. It's just a total crash, and I have all these huge initiatives hanging in the air now, and I just... I can't do it anymore.

During that time when you were working so intensely, did you feel unusually high, euphoric, or irritable—like you didn’t need sleep or that you had special abilities or ideas that were bigger than everyone else's?

Yes, exactly. I mean, at the very beginning of this whole... well, I call it an assignment, but it was really just me deciding to take over everything... I felt, I don't know, almost electrically upbeat. It was this incredible buzzing feeling, like I was plugged straight into the main power line of the plant. I’d walk the assembly floor and just see all the inefficiencies, all the bottlenecks, and I felt so incredibly good and energized about fixing them right then and there. 

But then, it didn't stay just upbeat. It morphed into this... I got so weirdly irritable. Like, intensely, out-of-nowhere irritable. Because, you know, in industrial engineering, there are mathematically right ways to do things to optimize throughput, and I could suddenly see the perfect way to fix our entire system. And when I would roll out these ideas, if anyone even hesitated—like if the floor supervisor asked a simple question about the new shift rotations, or if a vendor told me they couldn't expedite a shipment of raw aluminum—I would just internally explode. 

It honestly felt like anyone questioning my ideas was just slowing down something that was so completely obvious and important. I couldn't understand why they couldn't see the big picture the way I was seeing it. It was like I was looking at this beautiful, perfect 3D model of how the plant should run, and they were all just dragging their feet, almost like they were doing it on purpose just to ruin this flawless system I was building. I had absolutely zero patience for it, which isn't normally like me at all. I'm usually very collaborative—we have safety committees and planning boards for a reason—but during those weeks, I just wanted to bypass all of them because every single question they asked just felt like this massive, insulting roadblock to progress.
Can you describe how long you felt that intense, electrically upbeat mood and high level of energy lasted before you started feeling the crash?

Well, the whole timeline is a bit tangled in my head now, but... okay, so if I trace it back, that whole intense overdrive phase—the buzzing, the non-stop planning, the snapping at everyone because they couldn't keep up with my vision—that probably went on for, I don't know, maybe four or five weeks? It felt like an eternity and a split second all at once. I was just running so hot for so long. 

But the crash... that intense shift from being in total overdrive to suddenly barely being able to function at all... that really started right around the time I moved into this temporary apartment. Which was about three weeks ago. My lease was up at my old place, and honestly, managing a move on top of everything else I was forcing onto my plate at the plant was just... it was the straw that broke the camel's back, I think. I remember the first night in the new place, surrounded by all these boxes that I had packed in this frantic, hyper-efficient frenzy just days before, and I just sat on the floor and stared at them. I couldn't even fathom opening one. And it's been like that ever since. For three weeks now, I've just been waking up in this unfamiliar apartment, feeling like my limbs are made of lead, and dreading going into the plant to face all the massive projects I started when I was feeling so electric. It's just been this heavy, paralyzing fog for three solid weeks.
During the past week, have you felt persistently sad, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or experienced changes in your appetite or sleep unrelated to your lack of energy?

Yeah, I mean... it's just this overwhelming sadness that I can't shake. It's not just the energy being gone, it's... it's like this deep, crushing weight. Lately I wake up in the temporary apartment with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the day is already ruined before I even drive to the plant. 

And it's weird because I used to love my mornings, you know? I'd get up, make my coffee, review some schematics or read up on new lean manufacturing techniques, and I'd feel ready to tackle the day. But now... now I just lie there in this strange bed, looking at the ceiling, and I feel so incredibly sad. It's this pervasive, dark cloud that just sits right on my chest. I don't care about the workflow optimizations anymore. I don't care about the CAD files or the shift schedules or any of the things that used to completely absorb me. 

Even things outside of work... I used to love going for a run after my shift to clear my head, or trying out new recipes—I'm usually really into meal prepping, very systematic about it, measuring everything out—but I haven't cooked a single thing since I moved. I just look at the stove and feel absolutely nothing. Well, not nothing, just... this profound emptiness. I'm barely eating because nothing sounds good, and the thought of chewing just seems exhausting and pointless. And my sleep is a total mess. I'm exhausted, like I said, dragging myself around, but when I actually try to sleep, I'll wake up at 3 AM and just lie in the dark, feeling this intense, hollow ache, just dreading the sun coming up because it means I have to face another day feeling this completely, utterly broken. It's just so heavy. Everything is just so heavy and sad.

During that intense period when you felt so energized and were working non-stop, did you go at least four full days without needing much sleep at all—like barely sleeping or feeling rested but still full of energy?

Oh, absolutely. It was way more than four days. It was... gosh, it felt like that entire month, honestly. I remember just looking at the clock, sitting at my kitchen island with my laptop open, running throughput simulations on the new assembly line layout, and suddenly it would be 3:00 AM. And I'd think, well, I guess I should lie down, just because that's what you're supposed to do. But I wouldn't even really sleep. I was sleeping maybe two or three hours, tops. 

And the crazy thing is, I wasn't waking up groggy at all. I'd pop out of bed at 5:00 or 5:30 AM and just feel completely electric again. I was showing up at the plant before the first shift even clocked in, feeling incredibly sharp and charged, ready to just go, go, go. It actually got to the point where I started viewing sleep as this massive design flaw in the human body. Like, I remember literally thinking to myself that sleep was just optional, or at the very least, grossly inefficient. I mean, think about it from a production standpoint—shutting down the main processor for eight hours a day? It made absolutely no sense to me at the time. 

So yeah, I was running on two or three hours a night for a solid stretch, day after day, and I didn't feel tired in the slightest. I just felt like I had finally unlocked this perfect, optimized version of myself where I didn't need to waste time resting when there was so much critical work to be done. I'd just drink a glass of water and head straight out the door, completely wired and ready to overhaul the entire floor plan.

This supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder with current episode depressed, and rules out major depressive disorder and other bipolar subtypes not otherwise specified.

The hypomanic episode included elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and irritability lasting for several weeks.
